concepts.name: Microscopes: magnification, resolution and measuring cells
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Light, transmission electron and scanning electron microscopes compared (resolution limits about 200 nm for the light microscope and about 0.5 nm for the TEM, as approximate values); definitions of magnification and resolution and why they differ; units mm, µm and nm and conversions; calculating magnification, image size and actual size from drawings, photomicrographs, electron micrographs and scale bars; calibrating an eyepiece graticule with a stage micrometer and measuring cells with it. Preparing slides and drawing cells are abio.cells.slides-and-cells.

concepts.name: Preparing slides and observing plant and animal cells
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Temporary preparations (wet mounts of onion epidermis and cheek cells, stains such as iodine and methylene blue and why they are used), observing and drawing plant and animal cells from slides and photomicrographs, describing and interpreting photomicrographs and electron micrographs of typical plant and animal cells, comparing plant and animal cells (cell wall, chloroplasts, large permanent vacuole, centrioles, plasmodesmata), and the statement that cells use ATP from respiration for energy-requiring processes. Organelle structure and function in detail is abio.cells.eukaryotic-ultrastructure; drawing conventions for the practical papers are abio.skills.biological-drawing.

concepts.name: Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure: organelles and their functions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Structure and function of the cell surface membrane, nucleus, nuclear envelope and nucleolus, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, mitochondria (with small circular DNA), ribosomes (80S cytoplasmic, 70S in mitochondria and chloroplasts), lysosomes, centrioles and microtubules, cilia, microvilli, chloroplasts (with small circular DNA), cell wall, plasmodesmata, the large permanent vacuole and tonoplast; recognising them in electron micrographs; how organelles work together (for example the secretion of a protein from rough ER through the Golgi body). Membrane structure is abio.membranes.fluid-mosaic.

concepts.name: Prokaryotic cells and viruses
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Key features of a typical bacterium (unicellular, about 1-5 µm, peptidoglycan cell wall, circular DNA, plasmids, 70S ribosomes, no double-membrane organelles; capsule, pili and flagella as optional features), comparison of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and viruses as non-cellular structures with a DNA or RNA core, a protein capsid and in some an envelope; whether viruses are alive. The three-domain classification and virus classification by nucleic acid are abio.biodiversity.classification-hierarchy.

concepts.name: Testing for biological molecules
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Benedict's test for reducing sugars, the non-reducing sugar test (acid hydrolysis, neutralising, Benedict's), the iodine test for starch, the emulsion test for lipids and the biuret test for proteins: method, positive and negative results and safety; the semi-quantitative Benedict's test (standardised method, time to first colour change or colour standards) and estimating concentration; the colorimeter for quantitative work (absorbance or transmission against a calibration curve).

concepts.name: Monosaccharides, disaccharides and the glycosidic bond
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Monomer, polymer, macromolecule, monosaccharide, disaccharide, polysaccharide; covalent bonds join monomers; ring forms of alpha- and beta-glucose (drawn and described); reducing sugars (glucose, fructose, maltose) and sucrose as a non-reducing sugar; formation of a glycosidic bond by condensation (maltose, sucrose, lactose) and its breakage by hydrolysis, linked to the non-reducing sugar test. Polysaccharides are abio.molecules.polysaccharides.

concepts.name: Polysaccharides: starch, glycogen and cellulose
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Molecular structure of amylose (alpha-1,4, helix), amylopectin and glycogen (alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 branches) and cellulose (beta-1,4, alternate glucose units inverted, hydrogen-bonded chains, microfibrils and fibres); how each structure suits its function (compact, insoluble, osmotically inactive storage; rapid hydrolysis at branch ends; tensile strength of cell walls).

concepts.name: Lipids: triglycerides and phospholipids
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Triglycerides as non-polar, hydrophobic molecules: glycerol, fatty acids (saturated and unsaturated) and ester bonds formed by condensation; functions related to structure (energy store, insulation, buoyancy, metabolic water, protection); phospholipids with a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails and why they form bilayers. The emulsion test is abio.molecules.tests; membranes are abio.membranes.fluid-mosaic.

concepts.name: Amino acids and the structure of proteins
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). General structure of an amino acid (amine, carboxyl, R group), formation and hydrolysis of a peptide bond, dipeptides and polypeptides; primary, secondary (alpha-helix, beta-pleated sheet), tertiary and quaternary structure; the interactions that hold proteins in shape (hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds); globular (generally soluble, physiological roles) and fibrous (generally insoluble, structural) proteins; denaturation. Haemoglobin and collagen in detail are abio.molecules.haemoglobin-collagen.

concepts.name: Haemoglobin and collagen: structure and function
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Haemoglobin as a globular protein: two alpha-globin and two beta-globin chains, a haem group with iron(II) in each, quaternary structure, hydrophilic outer R groups and solubility, and how the structure suits oxygen transport (the oxygen dissociation curve itself is abio.mammal-transport.gas-transport); collagen as a fibrous protein: three polypeptide chains in a triple helix with glycine at every third position, cross-links between molecules, staggered arrangement into fibrils and fibres, and how this gives tensile strength (tendons, skin, artery walls).

concepts.name: Water: structure, properties and roles
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The polar water molecule and hydrogen bonding between molecules; properties and their biological importance: solvent action (transport, reactions in solution), high specific heat capacity (stable temperatures in organisms and water bodies), high latent heat of vaporisation (cooling by sweating and transpiration), cohesion and surface tension, density maximum near 4 °C and ice floating; water as a reactant (hydrolysis, photosynthesis) and as an environment for organisms (ZIMSEC detail; for example life in Lake Kariba or the Zambezi).

concepts.name: How enzymes work
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Enzymes as globular proteins acting inside cells (intracellular) or secreted (extracellular); active site, enzyme-substrate complex, specificity, lowering of activation energy (energy profile described in words or a table of values); the lock-and-key and induced-fit hypotheses; following the progress of a reaction by product formation (catalase and oxygen volume) or substrate disappearance (amylase and the iodine test), initial rates from the tangent at time zero, and the colorimeter for reactions with a colour change.

concepts.name: Factors affecting the rate of enzyme-catalysed reactions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Effects of temperature (kinetic energy, optimum, denaturation), pH (ionic and hydrogen bonds, buffer solutions), enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on rate, with explanations and the shapes of the graphs described in words and as tables; designing and analysing investigations (rates as 1/time, controls, standardised variables); Q10 is NOT required. Inhibitors, Vmax and Km are abio.enzymes.inhibition-kinetics.

concepts.name: Enzyme inhibition, Vmax, Km and immobilised enzymes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Reversible competitive and non-competitive inhibition (effects of inhibitor and substrate concentration on rate); irreversible inhibition and poisons such as cyanide, mercury and other heavy metals and some insecticides (ZIMSEC detail; organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase); Vmax and the Michaelis-Menten constant Km as a measure of affinity and how competitive and non-competitive inhibitors change them (Cambridge detail); enzymes immobilised in alginate beads compared with free enzymes, and the advantages of immobilisation (Cambridge detail). End-product inhibition only as an extension.

concepts.name: The fluid mosaic model of membranes and cell signalling
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The phospholipid bilayer and why it forms (hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions); arrangement and roles of cholesterol, glycolipids, intrinsic and extrinsic proteins (channel and carrier proteins, receptors) and glycoproteins in stability, fluidity, permeability, transport, cell signalling and cell recognition (antigens); the outline of cell signalling: ligands secreted, transported and bound to cell surface receptors. The cAMP cascade is abio.homeostasis.blood-glucose.

concepts.name: Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Simple diffusion and the factors affecting its rate, facilitated diffusion through channel and carrier proteins, osmosis in terms of water potential (pure water 0, solutions negative; knowledge of solute and pressure potential not expected), effects on animal cells (lysis, crenation) and plant cells (turgid, flaccid, plasmolysed); investigations with Visking tubing and plant tissue (potato cylinders or onion epidermis), serial dilutions, percentage change in mass and estimating the water potential of a tissue from the zero-change intercept.

concepts.name: Active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Active transport against a concentration gradient by carrier proteins using ATP (the sodium-potassium pump as an example), evidence such as respiratory inhibitors and temperature effects, endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis) and exocytosis (secretion of enzymes and hormones, neurotransmitters), comparing all the transport processes in a table.

concepts.name: Surface area to volume ratio and diffusion
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). Calculating surface areas and volumes of cubes, cuboids and cylinders and the SA:V ratio; why SA:V decreases as size increases and the consequences for diffusion and the need for exchange surfaces and transport systems; the agar block investigation (agar with indicator in acid or alkali, timing colour change, percentage of block coloured).

concepts.name: Chromosomes and the cell cycle
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Chromosome structure (DNA, histone proteins, sister chromatids, centromere, telomeres); the cell cycle: interphase (G1 growth, S phase DNA replication, G2), mitosis and cytokinesis; the role of telomeres in preventing loss of genes during replication; stem cells and their role in cell replacement and tissue repair by mitosis (totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent in outline). Stages of mitosis are abio.division.mitosis; cancer is abio.division.cancer.

concepts.name: Mitosis: stages and significance
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Behaviour of chromosomes, nuclear envelope, cell surface membrane, centrioles and spindle in prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase; cytokinesis in animal cells (cleavage furrow) and plant cells (cell plate); identifying stages in photomicrographs, diagrams and slides (onion or garlic root tip squash), mitotic index and estimating the relative duration of stages; the importance of mitosis (growth, replacement, repair, asexual reproduction, genetically identical cells).

concepts.name: Uncontrolled cell division and cancer
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). How uncontrolled mitosis forms a tumour (benign and malignant, metastasis); mutations in genes that control the cell cycle (proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes in outline); carcinogens (tobacco smoke, some chemicals such as aflatoxins, ionising and ultraviolet radiation, some viruses such as HPV) and other risk factors; the stages in the development of cancer in outline; prevention, screening and treatment principles (no statistics unless widely documented).

concepts.name: Meiosis: reduction division
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Haploid (n) and diploid (2n), homologous pairs of chromosomes, the need for a reduction division in gamete production; behaviour of chromosomes, nuclear envelope, cell membrane and spindle in prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I and meiosis II (sub-divisions of prophase I not needed); identifying stages in photomicrographs and diagrams (anther squashes, pollen grain formation); comparing mitosis and meiosis in a table. How meiosis produces variation is abio.division.genetic-variation.

concepts.name: How meiosis and fertilisation produce genetic variation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Crossing over between non-sister chromatids at chiasmata in prophase I, random (independent) orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I and of sister chromatids at metaphase II, calculating the number of possible chromosome combinations (2^n), and random fusion of gametes at fertilisation producing genetically different individuals; the importance of variation for natural selection.

concepts.name: Nucleotides and the structure of DNA and RNA
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Nucleotide structure (pentose sugar, phosphate, nitrogenous base) and nucleosides; ATP as a phosphorylated nucleotide; purines (adenine, guanine, double ring) and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil, single ring); formation of a dinucleotide and polynucleotide by phosphodiester bonds; the DNA double helix: antiparallel 5' to 3' and 3' to 5' strands, complementary base pairing, two hydrogen bonds in A-T and three in C-G; differences between DNA and RNA nucleotides and molecules; structure of mRNA (and tRNA in outline). Chargaff's rule calculations included.

concepts.name: Semi-conservative replication of DNA
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Semi-conservative replication in the S phase: unwinding and separation of strands, free nucleotides pairing, DNA polymerase adding nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction, leading and lagging strands (Okazaki fragments) and DNA ligase; the Meselson and Stahl experiment (heavy nitrogen 15N and light 14N, density bands after one and two generations) as evidence (ZIMSEC detail, useful to Cambridge), and why conservative and dispersive models were rejected. Other replication enzymes only by name if at all.

concepts.name: The genetic code and transcription
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). A gene as a sequence of nucleotides coding for a polypeptide; the universal, non-overlapping, degenerate triplet code with start and stop codons (using a codon table given in the question); transcription: RNA polymerase, the template (transcribed) strand and non-transcribed strand, complementary RNA nucleotides, the primary transcript; in eukaryotes, removal of introns and joining of exons (splicing) to form mRNA. Translation is abio.nucleic.translation.

concepts.name: Translation: from mRNA to polypeptide
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). mRNA leaving the nucleus, ribosome structure in outline, tRNA with its anticodon and amino acid attachment site (amino acid activation using ATP), initiation at the start codon, codon-anticodon pairing, peptide bond formation, ribosome movement, termination at a stop codon; polysomes; working out amino acid sequences from DNA or mRNA base sequences with a given table; the overall flow DNA → mRNA → polypeptide.

concepts.name: Gene mutations and their effects
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). A gene mutation as a change in the sequence of base pairs; substitution, deletion and insertion, frameshift, silent, missense and nonsense effects explained with original base sequences and a codon table; why some mutations have no effect (degenerate code, non-coding regions); sickle cell anaemia as an example of a substitution (GAG to GTG, glutamic acid to valine); mutagens and how mutation and environment together affect phenotype (ZIMSEC objective).

concepts.name: Xylem and phloem: structure and distribution
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Distribution of xylem and phloem in transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves of herbaceous dicotyledonous plants (and monocotyledonous roots and stems as a ZIMSEC comparison) and drawing plan diagrams from slides and photomicrographs; structure of xylem vessel elements (lignin, pits, no end walls, dead) and phloem sieve tube elements (sieve plates, few organelles) and companion cells (many mitochondria, plasmodesmata), and how each structure suits its function.

concepts.name: Water uptake: from soil to xylem
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Mineral ions and organic compounds transported dissolved in water; water entering root hair cells by osmosis; apoplast pathway (cellulose cell walls, lignin), symplast pathway (cytoplasm and plasmodesmata) and the vacuolar pathway (ZIMSEC); the endodermis, Casparian strip and suberin forcing water into the symplast; active loading of ions and root pressure (with the cut-stem observation). Movement up the xylem is abio.plant-transport.transpiration.

concepts.name: Transpiration and the movement of water in the xylem
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Transpiration as evaporation from internal leaf surfaces followed by diffusion of water vapour through stomata; factors affecting the rate and the potometer (measuring water uptake and calculating rates); cohesion-tension (hydrogen bonding), transpiration pull, adhesion to cellulose walls and capillarity; xerophytic adaptations with annotated descriptions of leaf sections (for example marram grass, and local examples such as aloes and euphorbias described accurately) and how each reduces water loss.

concepts.name: Translocation in the phloem
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Assimilates such as sucrose and amino acids moving from sources to sinks in sieve tubes; loading by companion cells using proton pumps and sucrose-proton cotransporter proteins; mass flow down a hydrostatic pressure gradient from source to sink (the mass flow hypothesis) and evidence for and against it (aphid stylets, ringing, radioactive tracers) in outline; comparison of xylem and phloem transport.

concepts.name: The circulatory system, blood vessels and tissue fluid
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). The closed double circulation (heart, arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins); functions of the pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, aorta and vena cava; structure of muscular arteries, elastic arteries, veins and capillaries related to function, with plan diagrams in TS and LS and recognition in slides and micrographs; red blood cells, monocytes, neutrophils and lymphocytes recognised and drawn; water as the main component of blood; formation and functions of tissue fluid and lymph in outline (Cambridge detail).

concepts.name: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Oxygen carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells; the oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin (cooperative binding and the S shape) and its importance at the partial pressures of the lungs and respiring tissues; the Bohr shift and its importance; carbon dioxide transport: carbonic anhydrase, hydrogencarbonate ions, haemoglobinic acid, carbaminohaemoglobin, the chloride shift and plasma; myoglobin and fetal haemoglobin curves compared with adult haemoglobin and why the differences matter (ZIMSEC detail, a useful extension for Cambridge).

concepts.name: The heart and the cardiac cycle
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). External and internal structure of the mammalian heart (chambers, valves, septum, coronary arteries), differences in wall thickness (atria and ventricles, left and right ventricles); the cardiac cycle with pressure changes in atria, ventricles and aorta during systole and diastole linked to the opening and closing of valves (pressure data in tables); heart rate and cardiac output calculations; myogenic initiation by the sinoatrial node, the atrioventricular node delay, the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue (nervous and hormonal control only in outline as a ZIMSEC extension).

concepts.name: Blood pressure, hypertension and the effects of exercise
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Systolic and diastolic blood pressure, measuring with a sphygmomanometer, readings in mmHg (for example 120/80 as a typical healthy adult reading), hypertension and its risk factors and consequences; normal resting pulse rate and measuring it; short-term and long-term effects of regular exercise on the cardiovascular system (larger stroke volume, lower resting heart rate, improved cardiac output and capillary networks) and what an efficient cardiovascular system means. No invented prevalence statistics.

concepts.name: The human gas exchange system
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). Structure of the lungs, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and capillary network; distribution of cartilage, ciliated epithelium, goblet cells, squamous epithelium, smooth muscle, elastic fibres and capillaries and recognising them in slides and micrographs, with plan diagrams of the trachea and bronchus wall; functions of ciliated cells, goblet cells and mucous glands in keeping the system healthy and of cartilage, smooth muscle, elastic fibres and squamous epithelium; gas exchange between alveolar air and blood by diffusion and the features that maximise it. Smoking diseases are not in the 2025-2027 syllabus except as context.

concepts.name: Cholera and tuberculosis
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Infectious disease as caused by transmissible pathogens; cholera (the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, transmission in faecally contaminated water and food, the toxin and diarrhoea in outline, oral rehydration, prevention by clean water, sanitation and vaccination) and tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. bovis, airborne droplets and unpasteurised milk, the link with HIV and crowding, BCG vaccination, DOTS and long courses of antibiotics, drug-resistant TB); biological, social and economic factors in prevention and control, including Zimbabwe's 2008-09 cholera outbreak described only with well-documented facts; global distribution of both diseases.

concepts.name: Malaria
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Pathogens (Plasmodium falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale, P. vivax: protoctists), transmission by female Anopheles mosquitoes, blood transfusion and from mother to fetus; global distribution and the link with climate and altitude (lowveld and Zambezi valley versus highveld in Zimbabwe described in general terms); prevention and control (insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, draining breeding sites, drugs and drug resistance, vaccines in outline) and the biological, social and economic factors that make control difficult. Details of the parasite's life cycle are not expected beyond an outline.

concepts.name: HIV and AIDS
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The human immunodeficiency virus (a retrovirus: RNA, reverse transcriptase, envelope) infecting T-helper cells and the progression to AIDS; transmission (unprotected sex, infected blood and needles, mother to child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding); prevention and control (condoms, testing, antiretroviral therapy reducing viral load, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, pre-exposure prophylaxis, voluntary medical male circumcision in outline, education and reducing stigma) and the biological, social and economic factors; global distribution with southern Africa as a highly affected region (no invented statistics). Treated factually and without stigma.

concepts.name: Epidemiology and the global distribution of disease
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 5). Epidemiological terms (incidence, prevalence, mortality, endemic, epidemic, pandemic) and evaluating epidemiological evidence from tables and maps described in words; global distribution and its causes for Ebola virus disease (transmission by body fluids, outbreaks in Central and West Africa, control by isolation and contact tracing), coronary heart disease (risk factors such as diet, smoking, inactivity and hypertension) and sickle cell anaemia (distribution overlapping historical malaria regions and heterozygote advantage). Cholera, malaria, TB and HIV have their own concepts.

concepts.name: Antibiotics and antibiotic resistance
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). How penicillin acts (inhibiting enzymes that build peptidoglycan cross-links so growing bacteria burst by osmotic lysis), why antibiotics do not affect viruses, the consequences of antibiotic resistance (untreatable infections, MRSA and drug-resistant TB as examples) and steps to reduce its impact (completing courses, not prescribing for viral infections, limiting use in livestock, infection control, new drug development). Resistance as natural selection is introduced here and developed in abio.evolution.natural-selection.

concepts.name: Drug and substance abuse
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 5). What a drug is and the difference between medicinal and recreational use; dependence and tolerance; biological effects of alcohol (liver, nervous system, foetal alcohol syndrome), nicotine and tobacco smoke, cannabis, methamphetamine and the misuse of codeine-containing cough syrups, all at a level of well-established medical fact; social and economic consequences and support for people who use drugs; no sensational claims and no invented statistics. Taught in a health-education, non-judgemental tone.

concepts.name: Phagocytes, lymphocytes and the immune response
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Non-specific defence by phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages: chemotaxis, engulfing, phagosome and lysosome fusion, digestion); antigens and the difference between self and non-self antigens; the primary immune response: antigen presentation by macrophages, clonal selection and expansion, B-lymphocytes and plasma cells secreting antibodies, T-helper cells (cytokines) and T-killer cells; memory cells, the secondary response (faster, larger) and long-term immunity, with antibody concentration data in tables. Antibody structure is abio.immunity.antibodies.

concepts.name: Antibodies and monoclonal antibodies
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Antibody structure (four polypeptide chains, two heavy and two light, disulfide bonds, constant and variable regions, antigen-binding sites, hinge region) related to functions (agglutination, neutralisation, opsonisation and attracting phagocytes, lysis); the hybridoma method for monoclonal antibodies and the principles of their use in diagnosis (for example pregnancy tests and rapid diagnostic tests for malaria described in outline) and in treatment (Cambridge detail).

concepts.name: Types of immunity and vaccination
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Active and passive immunity, natural and artificial immunity, with examples (infection, vaccination, antibodies across the placenta and in breast milk, injected antibodies or antitoxins); vaccines contain antigens (attenuated, inactivated, subunit or toxoid in outline) that stimulate memory cells; how vaccination programmes control the spread of infectious disease (herd immunity, the eradication of smallpox, measles, polio and the problems of antigenic variation, cold chains and coverage). No anti-vaccine framing; no invented coverage figures.

concepts.name: Energy and ATP
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The need for energy in living organisms (active transport, movement, anabolic reactions such as DNA replication and protein synthesis, maintaining body temperature in mammals and birds); ATP as a phosphorylated nucleotide and the features that suit it as the universal energy currency (small, soluble, energy released in small amounts by hydrolysis, easily regenerated); ATP synthesis by substrate-linked phosphorylation and by chemiosmosis in mitochondria and chloroplasts (principle only; detail in the respiration and photosynthesis concepts).

concepts.name: Glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Sites of the four stages of aerobic respiration; glycolysis: phosphorylation of glucose to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, splitting into two triose phosphates, oxidation to pyruvate with net ATP and reduced NAD; pyruvate entering the mitochondrion when oxygen is available; the link reaction (decarboxylation, dehydrogenation, coenzyme A and acetyl CoA); the Krebs cycle as oxaloacetate (4C) accepting acetyl (2C) to form citrate (6C) and regenerating oxaloacetate in small steps with decarboxylation, dehydrogenation, reduced NAD and FAD and substrate-linked ATP; counting carbons and products per glucose.

concepts.name: Oxidative phosphorylation and the mitochondrion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Roles of NAD and FAD in carrying hydrogen to carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane; hydrogen atoms splitting into protons and electrons, electrons releasing energy along the electron transport chain (carriers not named), protons pumped into the intermembrane space, chemiosmosis through ATP synthase (details of the enzyme not expected), oxygen as the final electron acceptor forming water; structure of the mitochondrion (outer and inner membranes, cristae, matrix, intermembrane space) related to function from diagrams and electron micrographs; effects of respiratory inhibitors such as cyanide in outline.

concepts.name: Anaerobic respiration
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Lactate fermentation in mammals (muscle, oxygen debt and lactate conversion in the liver) and ethanol fermentation in yeast and plants, with regeneration of NAD so glycolysis continues; why the energy yield of anaerobic respiration is much smaller than aerobic (a detailed ATP total is not expected); rice adaptations to submerged roots (aerenchyma, ethanol fermentation and tolerance, faster stem growth) (Cambridge detail); designing experiments to compare rates of fermentation of different sugars by yeast (ZIMSEC detail) and uses of fermentation in brewing and baking.

concepts.name: Respiratory substrates, RQ and respirometers
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Relative energy values of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins and why lipids release most energy per gram (more hydrogen atoms per molecule); the respiratory quotient (CO2 produced ÷ O2 taken in) and calculating RQ from equations (glucose 1.0, a typical lipid about 0.7, protein about 0.9) and from respirometer readings; simple respirometers with soda lime or potassium hydroxide, germinating seeds or small invertebrates (blowfly larvae; locally beetles or caterpillars such as madora, handled humanely), controls, readings and calculations of volume from a capillary meniscus (πr²l); investigating the effect of temperature on respiration rate with respirometers and with redox indicators (DCPIP, methylene blue) and yeast.

concepts.name: Chloroplasts and photosynthetic pigments
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Structure of the chloroplast (envelope, thylakoid membranes and spaces, grana, stroma, starch grains, lipid droplets, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes) related to function from diagrams and electron micrographs; sites of the light-dependent stage (thylakoids) and light-independent stage (stroma); chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotene and xanthophyll and their roles in light absorption; interpreting absorption spectra and action spectra; separating pigments by paper or thin-layer chromatography and calculating Rf values.

concepts.name: The light-dependent stage
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Photoactivation of chlorophyll in photosystems I and II; non-cyclic photophosphorylation (PSII and PSI, the oxygen-evolving complex and photolysis of water, electron transport, ATP and reduced NADP) and cyclic photophosphorylation (PSI only, ATP only); chemiosmosis across the thylakoid membrane (protons into the thylakoid space, back through ATP synthase); comparing cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation and comparing chemiosmosis in chloroplasts and mitochondria.

concepts.name: The Calvin cycle and C4 plants
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The light-independent stage: rubisco fixing carbon dioxide with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP, 5C) to give two glycerate 3-phosphate (GP, 3C), reduction of GP to triose phosphate (TP) using ATP and reduced NADP, regeneration of RuBP using ATP; uses of intermediates (GP for some amino acids; TP for carbohydrates, lipids and amino acids); effects of light and CO2 changes on GP and RuBP levels; C4 plants such as maize, sorghum and sugar cane (ZIMSEC detail): PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells, malate, Kranz anatomy, bundle sheath cells, avoiding photorespiration at high temperature and light.

concepts.name: Limiting factors and photosynthesis investigations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The concept of limiting factors (light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature; light wavelength) with graphs described in words and data in tables; investigations with whole aquatic plants (Elodea or Cabomba: counting bubbles or measuring gas volume, inverse square law for light intensity, hydrogencarbonate as a CO2 source), with leaf discs, and with redox indicators (DCPIP, methylene blue) and chloroplast suspensions for light intensity and wavelength; applications in greenhouses.

concepts.name: Principles of homeostasis
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). What homeostasis is and why it matters in mammals (core temperature, blood glucose concentration, blood water potential, with typical values as approximate); stimuli (internal and external), receptors, coordination by the nervous and endocrine systems, effectors (muscles and glands) and negative feedback (positive feedback only as a contrast); urea produced in the liver from the deamination of excess amino acids (in outline, no ornithine cycle detail).

concepts.name: The kidney: urine formation and osmoregulation
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Structure of the kidney (fibrous capsule, cortex, medulla, renal pelvis, ureter, branches of the renal artery and vein) and the nephron with its blood vessels (glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct) identified in diagrams and micrographs; ultrafiltration (podocytes, basement membrane, pressure) and selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule (microvilli, mitochondria, cotransport) related to structure; osmoregulation by the hypothalamus, posterior pituitary, ADH, aquaporins and the collecting duct as negative feedback. The countercurrent multiplier only in outline.

concepts.name: Control of blood glucose and cell signalling
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Negative feedback control of blood glucose: insulin from beta cells acting on muscle and liver cells (GLUT4 transporters, glycogenesis), glucagon from alpha cells acting on liver cells (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis); cell signalling by glucagon: receptor and conformational change, G-protein, adenylyl cyclase, the second messenger cyclic AMP, protein kinase A and the enzyme cascade amplifying the signal to activate glycogen phosphorylase; diabetes in outline; test strips and biosensors (glucose oxidase and peroxidase, colour change or electrical signal) for glucose in blood and urine.

concepts.name: Homeostasis in plants: stomata and guard cells
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Stomata balancing carbon dioxide uptake against water loss; daily rhythms of opening and closing; structure of guard cells (thickened inner walls, chloroplasts) and the mechanism of opening (proton pumping, potassium ion uptake, lowered water potential, water entry, turgor) and closing; abscisic acid in closing stomata during water stress, with calcium ions as a second messenger.

concepts.name: Communication systems: nervous and endocrine
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The need for communication systems in multicellular organisms; features of the endocrine system (glands, hormones in the blood, target cells and receptors) with ADH, glucagon and insulin as examples; comparing nervous and endocrine control (speed, duration, spread, transmission); structure and function of sensory, intermediate (relay) and motor neurones (cell body, dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier), drawn from prepared slides; reflex arcs in outline.

concepts.name: Receptors, resting potential and the action potential
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Sensory receptor cells as transducers detecting stimuli and starting impulses; the chemoreceptor in a human taste bud as the example (receptor potential, threshold, generator potential to action potential); the resting potential (about -70 mV) maintained by the sodium-potassium pump and differential permeability; the action potential: depolarisation by voltage-gated sodium channels, repolarisation by potassium channels, hyperpolarisation, the all-or-nothing principle; the refractory period and how the resting potential is restored; reading potential-against-time traces given as data.

concepts.name: Transmission of nerve impulses
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Local circuits and propagation of the action potential along an unmyelinated axon; the myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier and saltatory conduction; factors affecting speed (myelination, axon diameter, temperature) with speeds calculated from data; the importance of the refractory period in one-way transmission, discrete impulses and limiting impulse frequency; stimulus intensity coded by frequency.

concepts.name: The cholinergic synapse
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Structure of a cholinergic synapse (presynaptic knob, vesicles, synaptic cleft, postsynaptic membrane receptors) and how it works: arrival of an action potential, voltage-gated calcium channels and calcium ion influx, exocytosis of acetylcholine, binding to receptors, sodium entry and depolarisation, breakdown by acetylcholinesterase and recycling; roles of synapses (one-way transmission, summation in outline, integration); effects of drugs and poisons such as organophosphate insecticides and nicotine in outline.

concepts.name: Muscle contraction
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Neuromuscular junctions, the T-tubule system and sarcoplasmic reticulum in stimulating contraction of striated muscle; ultrastructure of striated muscle (myofibrils, sarcomere, Z lines, A and I bands, H zone, actin and myosin) from electron micrographs and diagrams; the sliding filament model with the roles of calcium ions, troponin, tropomyosin, myosin heads, cross-bridges and ATP; measuring sarcomere changes from data.

concepts.name: Control and coordination in plants
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). The rapid closure of the Venus fly trap (stimulation of sensory hairs, action potentials, ion movements and changes in turgor and cell walls, two stimuli needed); auxin in elongation growth by stimulating proton pumping to acidify cell walls (acid growth, expansins in outline); gibberellin in the germination of barley (embryo, aleurone layer, amylase synthesis, starch hydrolysis in the endosperm). Gibberellin and DELLA proteins at gene level are abio.inheritance.gene-control.

concepts.name: The gene concept: genes, proteins and phenotype
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The gene as the unit of inheritance at a locus on a chromosome, alleles, and how genes determine phenotype through the proteins they code for; examples: the TYR gene, tyrosinase and albinism; the HBB gene, beta-globin and sickle cell anaemia; the F8 gene, factor VIII and haemophilia; the HTT gene, huntingtin and Huntington's disease; the Le/le alleles and the gibberellin synthesis enzyme controlling stem height in peas; the history of the gene concept from Mendel in outline. Genetic crosses are abio.inheritance.monohybrid and later concepts.

concepts.name: Monohybrid inheritance
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Terms: gene, locus, allele, dominant, recessive, codominant, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, F1, F2, test cross; constructing and interpreting genetic diagrams and Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses involving complete dominance, codominance (for example roan coat colour in cattle) and multiple alleles (ABO blood groups); test crosses; relating genetic ratios to probabilities; pedigree charts interpreted. Sex linkage is abio.inheritance.sex-linkage.

concepts.name: Sex determination and sex linkage
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Sex chromosomes and sex determination in humans; sex-linked genes on the X chromosome; genetic diagrams for haemophilia and red-green colour blindness with carriers; pedigree analysis of sex-linked conditions; why males are more often affected; sex linkage combined with an autosomal gene in outline.

concepts.name: Dihybrid inheritance
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Dihybrid crosses with unlinked genes: gametes, Punnett squares, the 9:3:3:1 ratio from two heterozygotes and the 1:1:1:1 ratio from a dihybrid test cross; dihybrid crosses involving codominance or multiple alleles; relating expected ratios to probabilities. Autosomal linkage and epistasis are abio.inheritance.linkage-epistasis; testing results is abio.inheritance.chi-squared.

concepts.name: Autosomal linkage and epistasis
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Autosomal linkage: genes on the same chromosome inherited together, the effect on dihybrid ratios, crossing over producing recombinant offspring; epistasis as one gene affecting the expression of another, interpreted from genetic diagrams with the ratios worked out (knowledge of the ratios of different types of epistasis is not expected); recognising linkage or epistasis from unexpected ratios.

concepts.name: The chi-squared test in genetics
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Null hypotheses for genetic crosses; calculating expected numbers from a ratio; the chi-squared statistic Σ(O − E)²/E (formula provided in Cambridge papers); degrees of freedom (classes − 1); using a table of critical values at p = 0.05 to accept or reject the null hypothesis and stating the conclusion in words; one row or column of data only; ZIMSEC: interpreting chi-squared results (detailed computation is not required in Paper 4 but is practised for understanding); every value computed in code.

concepts.name: Control of gene expression
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Structural and regulatory genes; repressible and inducible enzymes; the lac operon in E. coli (promoter, operator, structural genes lacZ, lacY, lacA, the repressor protein and its gene, lactose as inducer; the role of cAMP is not expected); transcription factors in eukaryotes increasing or decreasing transcription; gibberellin causing the breakdown of DELLA proteins, which normally inhibit transcription factors, so that genes for growth and amylase are expressed.

concepts.name: Variation: genetic and environmental causes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Phenotypic variation caused by genes, by the environment or by both, with examples (height and mass, skin colour, ABO blood groups, plant growth with nutrients); discontinuous variation (few genes, distinct categories) and continuous variation (polygenes with additive effects plus environment) and their genetic basis; histograms and normal distributions of continuous data; how mutation and environmental factors such as diet, light and temperature affect phenotype. Statistical comparison is abio.evolution.t-test.

concepts.name: Comparing two means: the t-test
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). When the t-test is appropriate (continuous, approximately normally distributed data from two samples with similar standard deviations); null hypothesis; calculating sample means, standard deviations and t = (x̄1 − x̄2)/√(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2) (formula provided); degrees of freedom n1 + n2 − 2; comparing with a critical value at p = 0.05 and concluding in words; partly completed calculations as in Papers 4 and 5; every value computed in code.

concepts.name: Natural selection
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Overproduction of offspring, competition and the struggle for existence, variation, survival and reproduction of the best adapted and the passing on of their alleles; environmental factors as selection pressures; stabilising, directional and disruptive selection with examples and distributions described; antibiotic resistance in bacteria as an example of natural selection (mutation, selection, vertical and horizontal gene transfer in outline), insecticide resistance in mosquitoes and the sickle cell allele in malarial regions.

concepts.name: Allele frequencies: genetic drift, founder effect and Hardy-Weinberg
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). How selection, the founder effect, genetic drift and the bottleneck effect change allele frequencies, with examples (northern elephant seals and cheetahs as bottleneck examples); the Hardy-Weinberg principle: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (equations provided), the conditions under which it applies (large population, random mating, no mutation, migration or selection), and calculating allele, genotype and carrier frequencies from data; every value computed in code.

concepts.name: Artificial selection (selective breeding)
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Principles of selective breeding (choosing parents with desired traits, many generations, loss of genetic diversity and inbreeding depression); examples: introducing disease resistance into wheat and rice varieties, inbreeding and hybridisation to produce vigorous, uniform hybrid maize (as grown widely in Zimbabwe), improving milk yield in dairy cattle (progeny testing, artificial insemination); comparison with natural selection and with genetic engineering.

concepts.name: Evolution and speciation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Evolution as the formation of new species from pre-existing species by changes in gene pools over generations; how natural selection may bring about evolution; DNA sequence data (and protein sequence data) as evidence of evolutionary relationships, with counting differences in given sequences; speciation by genetic isolation: allopatric (geographical separation) and sympatric (ecological and behavioural separation, polyploidy in outline); reproductive isolating mechanisms; the species concept itself is abio.biodiversity.classification-hierarchy.

concepts.name: Classification, species and the domains of life
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Species concepts (biological, morphological, ecological) and their limitations; the taxonomic hierarchy kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; binomial nomenclature and its rules (genus capitalised, both names italicised or underlined); the three domains Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya and the differences between Archaea and Bacteria (membrane lipids, ribosomal RNA, cell wall composition) (Cambridge detail); classifying viruses by nucleic acid type and whether it is single- or double-stranded (Cambridge detail); dichotomous keys.

concepts.name: The kingdoms of life and their diagnostic features
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Diagnostic features of the kingdoms: Prokaryotae (ZIMSEC five-kingdom scheme), Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia; using diagnostic features to divide kingdoms into major phyla (for example flowering plants and conifers, ferns and mosses; arthropods, chordates, molluscs, annelids, flatworms, cnidarians) and identifying organisms from features (ZIMSEC detail); how the five-kingdom scheme relates to the three domains.

concepts.name: The socio-economic importance of the five kingdoms
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Prokaryotae (fermentation, biotechnology, food spoilage, decomposition, disease), Protoctista (Plasmodium and malaria, Trypanosoma and sleeping sickness, Schistosoma and bilharzia: note that Schistosoma is a flatworm in Animalia although the syllabus lists it here), Fungi (fermentation, penicillin, decomposition, food spoilage, food such as mushrooms), Plantae (producers, carbon sinks, timber, medicinal plants, tourism) and Animalia (tourism, food, hunting, leather, fishing such as kapenta on Lake Kariba), with Zimbabwean examples and no invented figures.

concepts.name: Ecosystems, niches and the levels of biodiversity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Definitions of species, habitat, population, niche, community and ecosystem with examples; biodiversity assessed at three levels: the number and range of ecosystems and habitats, the number of species and their relative abundance (species richness and evenness), and genetic variation within species; why genetic diversity matters. Sampling methods are abio.biodiversity.sampling.

concepts.name: Sampling to assess distribution and abundance
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Why random sampling matters and how to do it (random numbers on a grid); frame quadrats (percentage cover, frequency, density, species counts), line and belt transects along environmental gradients, and mark-release-recapture with the Lincoln index N = n1 × n2 ÷ m2 (formula provided) and its assumptions; designing a sampling investigation and estimating population size; every value computed in code.

concepts.name: Simpson's index and correlation
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Simpson's index of diversity D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² (formula provided), calculating it from sample data and interpreting values between 0 and 1; Pearson's linear correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (formulae provided): when each is appropriate, ranking data with ties, comparing with critical values, correlation from −1 to +1 and the difference between correlation and causation; examples relating biotic and abiotic factors to species distribution; every value computed in code.

concepts.name: The nitrogen cycle
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in legume root nodules (and free-living bacteria, lightning and the Haber process in outline), ammonification by decomposers, nitrification by Nitrosomonas (ammonium to nitrite) and Nitrobacter (nitrite to nitrate), denitrification by Pseudomonas and Clostridium in waterlogged, anaerobic soils, assimilation by plants; agricultural importance (groundnuts, soya and legumes in rotation, fertilisers, leaching and eutrophication).

concepts.name: Human impact on ecosystems
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Effects of human settlement, deforestation (tobacco curing and firewood as Zimbabwean drivers described in general terms), industrial activities, agriculture (fertilisers and eutrophication, pesticides, soil erosion), mining (gold panning and river siltation, acid drainage), global warming (greenhouse gases, effects on rainfall and species) and invasive plant species (for example water hyacinth and Lantana camara); case-study approach with original data only.

concepts.name: Threats to biodiversity and conservation strategies
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Why populations and species become extinct (climate change, competition, hunting by humans, degradation and loss of habitats) and reasons for maintaining biodiversity (ecological, economic, medicinal, aesthetic and ethical); conservation as preservation, management and reclamation with examples; conserved areas such as national parks and marine parks, zoos, botanic gardens, frozen zoos and seed banks; assisted reproduction in endangered mammals (IVF, embryo transfer, surrogacy) (Cambridge detail).

concepts.name: Conservation in Zimbabwe: elephants, rhinos, EMA and CAMPFIRE
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). The roles of the Environmental Management Agency (EMA) and the CAMPFIRE programme (community-based natural resource management); conservation of the African elephant (Loxodonta africana) and the white rhinoceros (Ceratotherium simum): reasons for concern (poaching for ivory and horn, habitat loss, human-wildlife conflict), measures (anti-poaching, dehorning, translocation, sanctuaries and conservancies), evaluating population trends from data given as original or clearly labelled approximate figures, international cooperation through CITES, conflicts of interest (ivory trade debates, crop damage, overpopulation of elephants in Hwange) and economic implications for Zimbabwe (tourism, hunting revenue).

concepts.name: Conservation organisations and invasive species
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and its Red List categories; CITES (what it is, its appendices in outline, how it regulates trade); reasons for controlling invasive alien species (competition, predation, disease, hybridisation, economic cost) with examples, and methods of control in outline.

concepts.name: Recombinant DNA and genetic engineering
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Recombinant DNA and genetic engineering defined; obtaining genes (extracted from donor DNA, made from mRNA by reverse transcriptase, synthesised chemically); restriction endonucleases and sticky ends, DNA ligase, plasmid vectors, DNA polymerase; why a promoter may be transferred with the gene; identifying transformed cells with marker genes coding for fluorescent products (GFP) (and antibiotic resistance markers in outline); gene editing as insertion, deletion or replacement of DNA at specific sites (CRISPR-Cas9 in outline).

concepts.name: Producing human insulin and other recombinant proteins
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The steps in producing human insulin by bacteria (obtaining the gene or making cDNA from mRNA, inserting into plasmids, transforming bacteria, selecting, culturing in fermenters, extracting and purifying); advantages of recombinant human insulin over insulin from animals for treating diabetes; other recombinant human proteins: factor VIII for haemophilia and adenosine deaminase for ADA deficiency (Cambridge detail).

concepts.name: PCR, gel electrophoresis and genetic fingerprinting
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The polymerase chain reaction (denaturation at about 95 °C, primer annealing at about 55-65 °C, extension at about 72 °C, Taq polymerase and why it is used, doubling per cycle with copy numbers computed); gel electrophoresis separating DNA fragments by length (negative DNA moving towards the anode, agarose gel, markers and estimating fragment size); the theoretical basis and process of genetic fingerprinting (variable tandem repeats, restriction or PCR, electrophoresis, comparing band patterns) and its uses in forensics and paternity (ZIMSEC detail).

concepts.name: Microarrays and bioinformatics databases
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). How DNA microarrays are used to analyse genomes and to detect mRNA in studies of gene expression (fluorescent labelling, hybridisation, reading spots) in outline; the benefits of databases of nucleotide sequences, genomes, amino acid sequences and protein structures (comparing sequences, identifying genes, studying evolution, designing drugs).

concepts.name: Genetic screening and genetic counselling
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). What genetic screening is and how it is carried out (testing adults, embryos and fetuses; amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling in outline; pre-implantation diagnosis); its roles and advantages with the examples of breast cancer (BRCA1 and BRCA2), Huntington's disease and cystic fibrosis (and sickle cell anaemia as a ZIMSEC-relevant example); the need for genetic counselling; social and ethical considerations of screening.

concepts.name: Gene therapy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The basis of gene therapy: adding functional alleles to cells using vectors (viruses, liposomes); somatic and germ-line therapy and why germ-line therapy is not permitted in humans in most countries; examples: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID, ADA deficiency) and inherited eye diseases (for example Leber congenital amaurosis); problems (short-lived effects, immune responses, insertion risks); social and ethical considerations.

concepts.name: Genetically modified organisms in agriculture: benefits and hazards
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). How genetic engineering may help to meet the demand for food: GM salmon (growth hormone gene and promoter), herbicide-resistant soybean, insect-resistant (Bt) cotton; general benefits and hazards of gene technology (yields, reduced pesticide use, medical products versus gene flow to wild relatives, resistance in pests and weeds, effects on non-target organisms, economic dependence on seed companies); ethical and social implications of GMOs in food production; Zimbabwe's cautious regulation of GM crops mentioned only in general, factual terms.

concepts.name: Social and ethical implications of gene technology
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). A balanced discussion of the social and ethical issues raised by gene technology as a whole: medicine (screening, designer babies, gene therapy, insurance and privacy), agriculture (food safety, farmers' rights, patents), forensic DNA databases and consent, and religious and cultural viewpoints; building and evaluating arguments for and against, as in ZIMSEC essay questions. No partisan conclusions; views attributed to groups, not invented individuals.

concepts.name: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Anther structure (epidermis, fibrous layer, tapetum, pollen sacs) and pollen formation by meiosis and mitosis (microspore mother cell, tetrad, generative and tube nuclei); ovule structure and development of the embryo sac (megaspore mother cell, meiosis, three mitotic divisions, egg cell, synergids, antipodals, polar nuclei); pollination in outline; double fertilisation (one male nucleus with the egg forming the zygote, the other with the polar nuclei forming the triploid endosperm nucleus) and its significance; the transverse section of an ovary observed and drawn.

concepts.name: Gametogenesis and its hormonal control
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Microscopic structure of the testis (seminiferous tubules, Sertoli cells, interstitial (Leydig) cells) and ovary (follicles at different stages, corpus luteum); spermatogenesis and oogenesis (germinal epithelium, mitosis, growth, meiosis I and II, spermatids and spermatozoa; primary and secondary oocytes, polar bodies, meiosis completed at fertilisation) compared; hormonal control of gametogenesis by GnRH, FSH, LH and testosterone.

concepts.name: The menstrual cycle and reproductive hormones
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). The roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the menstrual cycle in detail, including negative and positive feedback, follicle development, ovulation, the corpus luteum and the endometrium; interpreting graphs of hormone concentrations described as data tables; the role of hormones in premenstrual tension, menopause and hormone replacement therapy, with benefits and risks stated cautiously.

concepts.name: Fertilisation and the placenta
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Capacitation, the acrosome reaction, fusion of membranes, the cortical reaction preventing polyspermy and the fusion of nuclei; implantation in outline; structure of the placenta (chorionic villi, maternal blood spaces, umbilical artery and vein) and its roles: exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients and wastes, transfer of antibodies, a barrier to some pathogens and substances (and its limits: HIV, alcohol, nicotine), and hormone production (hCG, oestrogen, progesterone).

concepts.name: Contraception, IVF and abortion: biology and ethics
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). How methods of contraception work biologically (barrier methods, hormonal pills, injections and implants, intrauterine devices, sterilisation, natural methods) with relative effectiveness in general terms; in vitro fertilisation (stimulating ovulation, collecting eggs, fertilisation in vitro, embryo transfer); abortion described biologically; balanced discussion of biological and ethical viewpoints, including religious and cultural views, without advocacy and without legal advice.

concepts.name: Carrying out practical investigations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Practical skills for ZIMSEC Paper 4 and Cambridge Paper 3: identifying independent and dependent variables, choosing a range and at least five values, replicates, controls and standardised variables; following instructions safely and assessing risk as low, medium or high; recording results in tables with headings and units, consistent decimal places and processed values; significant figures (same as or one more than the data); graphs, bar charts and histograms; describing trends, finding values from graphs, estimating concentrations from qualitative results; identifying anomalies, systematic and random errors and suggesting improvements.

concepts.name: Biological drawing and microscope work in the practical papers
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Plan diagrams (tissue layers in correct proportion, no cells drawn) and high-power drawings of cells (correct shapes, cell walls as double lines, observable contents only, no shading, sharp continuous lines, label lines ruled); drawing from slides and photomicrographs; recording observable similarities and differences between specimens in a table; counting cells or organelles in a field of view or grid; calculating actual sizes in the practical context (low and high power drawings for ZIMSEC Paper 4).

concepts.name: Planning, analysis and evaluation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Planning an investigation from a given context (prediction and hypothesis, variables, how to vary and measure them, serial and proportional dilutions with % (w/v) and mol dm⁻³ concentrations, controls, replicates, a logical method, a simple risk assessment); analysing given data (means, percentages, rates of change, percentage gain or loss, choosing an appropriate statistical test and justifying it, stating a null hypothesis, types of variable and data: nominal, ordinal, continuous); conclusions and their limits; evaluating methods, anomalies, replication, ranges and control of variables, validity and confidence.

concepts.name: Descriptive statistics and error bars
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Mean, median, mode and range; normal and non-normal distributions; sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)), standard error SE = s/√n and 95% confidence intervals x̄ ± 2SE (formulae provided); plotting standard deviation, standard error or 95% CI error bars and judging whether differences between means are likely to be significant from overlap; percentage error; every value computed in code.
